name: Nora Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the optical-lens grinding line and check the first polished lens against its prescription. I have a two-year technical diploma and am among the best at finding a wheel vibration or a poor edge. I like teaching a new worker the gauge; I dislike sending an almost-right lens to someone who needs it to see.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Sam drives deliveries part-time, and our grown children live separately. We pay a house loan, my lead wage is low for this job, we have two weeks saved and only a few similar optical plants nearby. I use AI every day to sort defect notes, then check each result against a measured lens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can tidy the order book, but a lens still has to fit its prescription. I check the first ground lens against the gauge before the polishing machine runs a batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the lens-grinding shift and can recognise a chatter mark by touch, yet our pay is low for that responsibility. My husband Sam drives deliveries part-time, our grown children have their own lives, and we have two weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the grinding shift and use my daily AI notes to group defects, checking each summary against the measured lens. I would pay a little extra from a full new wage toward our house loan only after food and utilities were covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, even with little AI change. A cracked car tyre would use money meant for the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a chatter mark?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faint wave along the lens edge tells me the wheel shook. I stop the grinder before that wave reaches a whole tray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does AI enter the day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it every day to sort fault notes, but the lens gauge gives the answer. A tidy list is not a measured prescription.

Pay extra **house-loan principal** from fresh full wages after bills.
feel: **Anxious** about ordinary bills with a thin reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that new optical scanners should be tried on rejected lenses before anyone puts them in charge of a live order. I would learn one early if it catches a defect that my gauge also finds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot feeder could remove a person from my grinding shift, and I might lose paid hours even as lead. Two weeks saved and only a few optical shops nearby make that a household risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request an offered paid guarded practice slot on the stopped grinder with the setter beside me. If approved, I would learn the new AI defect scanner on rejected lenses and compare flags with gauge readings; after actual hour cuts, I would apply for posted reachable optical work only where net pay after travel covers our loan and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about hours and still keen to test the scanner. The first lens is a better judge than a sales sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust an AI flag alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We would test old rejected lenses with the wheel isolated, then compare every flag with a gauge before a live change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you take a different shop job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a real posting shows paid hours and enough after the trip. There are not many shops close enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2028 finds me sixty; capable lens-handling robots around 2031 find me sixty-three. The order desk changes before the grinder floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the factory to close my grinding shift once robots can load, inspect and polish lenses. Sam’s part-time deliveries and two weeks saved cannot carry the house loan, and I lie awake worrying about the next instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for written staffing dates and postpone replacing the family car. I would apply for posted reachable lens or quality roles only with bill-covering pay after travel and would not leave before a real offer and start date; if the shift ends without one, I would ask the lender about temporary terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed by the likely loss of most of my wage. A perfect lens will not read the loan reminder for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if verified retirement income and Sam’s confirmed pay covered housing, food and health costs. We have not seen figures that prove it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could grown children cover the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. I might ask for a lift to an interview, but not put their wages in our budget.

fieldNote: Expected **shift closure** supports alarm despite her senior technical skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2031 reaches me at sixty-three, and capable optical robots around 2034 at sixty-six. Five years could buy a real paid apprenticeship in machine calibration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know when a grinding wheel is wrong, but calibration work needs its own current qualification and supervised practice. Unpaid class hours would threaten the loan, and a certificate is worth little without a posted reachable job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid grinding shifts and ask the plant for a funded calibration course during paid time. If offered an actual place with the grinder isolated, a qualified calibrator supervising and a posted reachable role at bill-covering net pay after travel, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about our thin cash cushion but glad to test a genuine path. I can teach a new worker the lens gauge, and I can still be a learner myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A calibrator would isolate the spindle and supervise a gauge check on a training wheel. I would not adjust a live grinder for class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If no place appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts and compare posted optical jobs after hour cuts. I would not buy private training with loan money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight, and capable lens robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. Ten years gives Sam and me time to price the loan and our actual retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had hoped to stop full-time shifts at sixty-seven, but two weeks saved and a house loan do not fund that hope. I do not know any pension amount or Sam’s future delivery hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the paid grinding shift and pay a little extra loan principal from fresh full wages only after essentials. I would request retirement and loan figures; if verified income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven I would stop factory work then, otherwise continue safe paid work, and after 2036 compare posted reachable bill-covering work only if still employed and hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious despite the long warning because the next loan payment is due now. I want a last shift that does not turn our children into our bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the figures are short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep safe paid work and compare real posted wages after travel if shifts fell. I would not leave on an unpriced pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes and responsibilities. I would share our decision with them, not count their wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because lens robots around 2031 could close my grinding shift while the loan remains. Written staffing dates, offered funded paid safe calibration training and posted reachable work at bill-covering pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gauges the first polished lens before a whole tray is released. I would rather stop one wheel than explain a hundred wrong prescriptions.

headlineQuote: I would rather stop one wheel than explain a hundred wrong prescriptions.
portrait: **Nora**, 58, leads optical-lens grinding with a two-year technical diploma and exceptional fault-finding skill.
Her **low lead pay**, part-time delivery-driver husband Sam, grown children, house loan, two-week reserve and few nearby plants constrain her.
She uses **AI daily** for notes and would learn a new scanner only through offered paid guarded practice.
Expected **2031 shift closure** alarms her; a planned age-sixty-seven exit requires verified income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because 2031 lens robots may close her shift while the house loan remains.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded paid safe training and posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work would help.
